content: docs#Ordinal.le_mul_left is 0 < b → a ≤ a * b while docs#Cardinal.le_mul_left is b ≠ 0 → a ≤ b * a.
Which one is "correct"?
I'm inclined to say that either the left is the correct one, or that it's actually a mix of both b ≠ 0 → a ≤ a * b.
Oh and to make matters worse, a is explicit in the former but implicit in the latter
I have no preference there, but I'd still like these theorems to be consistent with each other
docs#Nat.le_mul_of_pos_left is some other precedence
Annoyingly docs#le_mul_left is some other statement!
Hm, should both of these statements be renamed to le_mul_of_pos_left and made to match the Nat statement then?
docs#le_mul_of_one_le_left' seems to be the general spelling
docs#Cardinal.le_mul_left and docs#Ordinal.le_mul_left are the opposite way around. Which one is it?
...oh my god did I really ask the same question twice? That's embarassing. I'll just make the PR to fix it.
#36890
Is pos supposed to be a prefix or a postfix? We have Real.pi_pos, but apparently le_mul_of_pos_left. I would have thought it to be le_mul_of_left_pos.
We certainly have precedent for pos_left and such, see docs#mul_pos_iff_of_pos_left and the surrounding lemmas
I think the idea is supposed to be that the lemma is actually le_mul_of_pos, version left
Hmm, I'd rather think of it as saying that the left is positive. That gives a lot more information about what the lemma means.
Otherwise I would have no idea which is left and which is right.
I think @Yaël Dillies is the one who best understands this left/right naming scheme.
Or should it be of_left_ne_zero?
Yeah, I vaguely remember the convention that hypotheses should be in the easier-to-prove form when possible. In this case non-zeroness is "weaker" than positivity.
So, is the solution here to change docs#Nat.le_mul_of_pos_left ?
Since it is in core, maybe it's more annoying to deprecate it, but at least we can add Nat.le_mul_of_left_ne_zero.

Hmm, there's also docs#le_mul_self and docs#le_self_mul ... and docs#self_le_mul_left and docs#self_le_mul_right which only differ in explicitness!? I kinda like the le_self_mul name because with the idea that self means "a variable that occurred before" it's pretty obvious what it means. le_mul_self on the other hand... well docs#Nat.le_mul_self means n ≤ n * n instead. For the other ones I guess you can also think about self_le_mul_left as self ≤ (a * ·) self ("self le left multiplication applied to self"), so maybe <op>_left should mean "the left side of <op> is a variable that didn't occur before"? I guess that would also be consistent with docs#mul_le_mul_left.

... and then we have docs#mul_left_mono (which takes MulRightMono!) that breaks this idea (but perhaps that just indicates that it's misnamed? I would think the right name would be mul_right_monotone).
MulRightMono is misnamed indeed. However, it should also be refactored: it should be a structure rather than an abbrev for performance reasons.
You think MulRightMono is the one that's misnamed...?
I guess without a proper convention you can argue both ways...
I defer to Yaël on all this. I remember a lot of lefts and rights switched around some six months ago and I still fail to remember what the precise convention is now.
We have a convention, and mul_left_mono was fixed 6 months ago, but MulRightMono was not yet fixed.
The convention in these monotonicity lemmas like mul_le_mul_left and mul_left_mono is that the left refers to the changing argument, i.e. the argument in which multiplication is monotone.
... and if we ignore the Monotone part, then mul_left would also be the naming for fun x => x * a under the logic that x is "more variable" than a?
I think fun x => x * a is called mul_const (see docs#Set.image_const_mul_Iic)

Why is it not mul_const_mono or const_mul_mono then?! Well I guess you could argue that both are fine..? The reason I'm asking is that it would be nice to have some more general algorithm you could apply to say whether left or right would be fine in a specific position; and ideally mul_left_mono etc. would just come automatically from there.
See #mathlib4 > left and right @ 💬 where I compiled a list of left and right
